Because as soon as you do, as soon as you start looking outside yourself for why your students are the way they are, you undermine your ability to do anything about it.
Taking responsibility for everything that happens in your classroom, on the other hand, is deeply empowering.

t: Are You Focusing On The Wrong Students?
q: A second group of students would emerge from the mist. This group, numbering between six and eight, but occasionally more, are the real source of the problem.
They are the oxygen that fuels the incitement of the few. They are the poor role models, the laughers of jokes, and the creators of tension.
The truth is, your difficult students don’t need any extra time or attention from you.
This idea that one or two students are creating most, or all, of the trouble and misbehavior in your classroom is a fallacy.
From the first day of school onward you must teach, model, and require exceptional behavior from all students. You must lock it down and button it up.
As your happy crew gets larger and larger, and the feeling of being part of something special grows stronger and stronger, no one will be able to resist its gravitational pull.

t: The Mental Reset Button - Hit It
q: We all make The List. This is because we are professionals, and a professional's work is never done.
But great professionals are great people leading great lives. That last word is important. So how do you plan to hit “Reset” on your professional brain before you tackle The List?
Too many great educators pretend that they can just power themselves through the last weeks of school and then plow straight into tackling The List. Don’t fool yourself; you need to reset.

Essentially, the overnighter is about doing everything but thinking about The List: we enjoy food, laughter, beer, and a campfire; we fish, we reminisce, we compete, we celebrate. Since we’re out in the middle of nowhere and staying the night, the constraints of time and space slip away as we mentally shift from the pressure of a school year into the decompression of summer break.

On the drive home the next morning, I always feel distinctly different than I did on the drive up. I’m excited for the summer, both its work and its relaxation. I’m thankful for the year that’s passed, free from any frustrations I was holding, and ready to start on The List in a more relaxed, refreshed fashion.
But some of you are like I was early on in my career — I glorified work. I felt like I had no time to reset or unplug.

t: $11,195 through Donors Choose - A Reflection on Generosity
q: During this past school year, a group of mostly strangers donated $4,197 worth of books to my classroom library ( here's the list ). I didn't earn a grant for this; I have no wealthy benefactors; and I didn't ask for donations from readers of this blog or its social networks.

Donors Choose has been around for twice as long now as it had been when I wrote my first project. People like Oprah and Stephen Colbert have promoted it since then. This means there are waaay more folks who are surfing Donors Choose looking to give to great classrooms.

The opportunities donors have given my kids really can't be quantified. Again and again, I've seen kids' minds light on fire — for some through whole-class readings of All Quiet on the Western Front or Things Fall Apart ; for others, through independent reading books from our classroom library; still for others, through some of the sweet tech Donors Choose has given us, like a podcast recorder or an iPad.

Unfortunately, technology is tricky. What I thought would be an easy marriage between the iPad and our school's existing technology was… well, not such an easy marriage. The iPad did serve some purposes in my room, but none as grand as I had hoped.

When I say responsibly, I mean only ask for stuff that you, in your professional judgment, believe will promote the long-term flourishing of your kids. Try to think through what could go wrong — not much can go wrong with books; plenty can go wrong with technology.

But with that said, if you've got a sweet vision for classroom resources that your kids need, it is smart to have a few lures in the water at all times. If your vision is huge, break it down into $100-$200 projects.

I don't know about you, but I can often get derailed by a single negative comment from a student, parent, or colleague. Yet every time I get one of those magical emails from Donors Choose saying, “Congratulations, your project is fully funded,” it's proof that, indeed, I am not alone in this.

t: A Trendy Classroom Management Strategy You Should Never Use you-should-never-use/
q: It’s a close cousin of the “caught being good” strategy, which we also don’t recommend, but is far more damaging to the targeted student.
You would give the students within proximity of the misbehaving student an enthusiastic pat on the back for not misbehaving.
It’s the classroom management version of a magician’s sleight of hand. But it’s cruel and dishonest and doesn’t help the student actually change their behavior.
It will make difficult students less inclined to get back on track in the future and turn your classroom into a petri dish of neediness, dependency, and underachievement.
Have a classroom management plan that clearly lays out the rules and consequences of the class.
What they really need is your honesty. They need your truth and forgiveness. They need your accountability, your leadership, and your consistency.
x: Linsin describes this as a manipulative and dishonest tactic, a close cousin of the 'caught being good' strategy, that offers the offending student no real feedback or opportunity to reflect on their misbehavior.
A trending district-encouraged strategy has teachers praise well-behaved students near a misbehaving student instead of addressing the misbehavior directly.
Linsin labels this tactic manipulative and dishonest, comparing it to a magician's sleight of hand that offers no real feedback or accountability to the offending student.
Over time it makes the offending student less likely to improve and can foster classroom-wide neediness and dependency.
The recommended alternative is a clear classroom management plan applied equally to all students, paired with honest, achievement-based praise and consistent follow-through.
